reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System Tumours
clinicalPearls: The most common primary malignant mesenchymal tumour of the liver, though still rare overall, arising from hepatic sinusoidal endothelial cells and behaving very aggressively.
Classically linked to environmental and occupational carcinogens, historically vinyl chloride monomer, arsenic and the former contrast agent thorotrast, though most modern cases are idiopathic.
Presentation is often non-specific with abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue and hepatomegaly, so diagnosis is frequently late.
Spontaneous tumour rupture causing haemoperitoneum is a well-recognised and potentially catastrophic mode of presentation.
Imaging typically shows multifocal hypervascular lesions with heterogeneous enhancement and areas of haemorrhage, and appearances can mimic haemangioma, leading to diagnostic delay.
Percutaneous biopsy carries a heightened bleeding risk owing to the vascular nature of the tumour and should be approached with caution.
Diagnosis rests on histology showing malignant endothelial cells lining irregular vascular channels, with immunohistochemical positivity for endothelial markers such as CD31, CD34 and ERG.
The tumour is chemoresistant and usually unresectable or metastatic at diagnosis; it is generally regarded as a contraindication to liver transplantation because of rapid recurrence.
reference.pathophysiology: Hepatic angiosarcoma originates from the malignant transformation of endothelial cells lining the hepatic sinusoids and small vessels. Recognised carcinogens, notably vinyl chloride monomer, inorganic arsenic and the radioactive contrast agent thorotrast, induce endothelial DNA damage and characteristic mutational signatures after prolonged latency, though the majority of contemporary cases lack an identifiable exposure. Neoplastic endothelial cells proliferate along and replace the sinusoidal framework, forming irregular, anastomosing vascular channels and solid spindle-cell areas that infiltrate and destroy hepatic plates. The abnormal, fragile neovasculature is prone to haemorrhage and thrombosis, accounting for the internal bleeding, necrosis and risk of spontaneous rupture, while the disorganised tumour vasculature can also sequester platelets and consume clotting factors, sometimes producing a consumptive coagulopathy.
additionalDifferentials: hypervascular metastases (for example from neuroendocrine tumour)
additionalInvestigations: multiphase contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen
MRI of the liver with contrast for lesion characterisation
image-guided biopsy with careful attention to bleeding risk
immunohistochemistry for CD31, CD34, ERG and factor VIII-related antigen
coagulation profile and platelet count to detect consumptive coagulopathy
staging CT of the chest to assess pulmonary metastases
redFlags: spontaneous tumour rupture with haemoperitoneum and haemodynamic collapse
rapidly progressive hepatomegaly with pain and weight loss
features of consumptive coagulopathy or unexplained bleeding
signs of hepatic decompensation or portal hypertension
new pulmonary or splenic lesions suggesting metastatic spread
reference.prognosis: Hepatic angiosarcoma has a dismal prognosis, with most patients surviving only months from diagnosis owing to late presentation, chemoresistance and frequent metastasis. Rare cases with a solitary resectable tumour and clear margins fare somewhat better but recurrence is common.
pitfalls: Misreading multifocal hypervascular lesions as benign haemangiomas and delaying diagnosis.
Performing unguarded percutaneous biopsy and precipitating major haemorrhage.
Overlooking a relevant occupational or thorotrast exposure history.
Listing the patient for transplantation, which is contraindicated by rapid recurrence.
Failing to recognise and correct an associated consumptive coagulopathy before intervention.
